title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
Q1: Why Minimize Squared Residuals?
A student proposes finding the best-fitting line by minimizing \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n e_i\) instead of \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2\). Explain why this approach fails.

Minimizing \(\sum e_i\) fails because positive and negative residuals cancel out.
Squaring the residuals:

prevents cancellation
penalizes large errors more heavily

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
Q2: Inference vs. Prediction
For each scenario, state whether the primary goal is inference or prediction and justify.
(a) A researcher wants to know whether students who attend more office hours tend to earn higher exam scores, and by roughly how many points per additional visit.

→ Inference. The goal is to understand the direction and magnitude of the relationship (how many points per visit), not just produce a predicted score.


(b) An app uses a patient’s age, weight, and exercise level to estimate their resting heart rate.
→ Prediction. The goal is an accurate individual estimate where the coefficient values are not the focus.

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
Q3: Errors vs. Residuals; Unbiasedness
The SLR model is \(y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i\).
(a) Explain the difference between the true error \(\varepsilon_i\) and the residual \(e_i\). Which one can we observe, and why?

\(\varepsilon_i\) is the true, unobservable error. It is the gap between \(y_i\) and the true line \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\).
\(e_i = y_i - \widehat{y}_i\) is the observable residual. It is the gap between \(y_i\) and the fitted line. We can compute \(e_i\) from data; \(\varepsilon_i\) requires knowing the unknown true parameters.

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
section: Q4–5: Computing and Interpreting the Model
text:
Q4–5: Computing and Interpreting the Model
A sports scientist records weeks of training (\(x\)) and one-mile run time in minutes (\(y\)) for \(n = 6\) runners. Given: \(\bar{x} = 7\), \(\bar{y} = 8\), \(S_{xx} = 70\), \(S_{xy} = -70\).
Compute \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_0\). (5, 3 pts) Write the fitted equation and interpret \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) in context.
Given \(S_{xy} = -70\), \(S_{xx} = 70\), \(\bar{x} = 7\), \(\bar{y} = 8\):
\[\widehat{\beta}_1 = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}} = \frac{-70}{70} = -1 \qquad \widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x} = 8 - (-1)(7) = 15\]

Fitted model: \(\quad\widehat{\text{time}} = 15 - 1 \cdot \text{weeks}\)
Interpretation of \(\widehat{\beta}_1 = -1\): Each additional week of training is associated with a predicted reduction of 1 minute in one-mile run time, on average.

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
Q8: RSS and \(\widehat{\sigma}^2\)
Compute RSS, \(\widehat{\sigma}^2\), and \(\widehat{\sigma}\). Interpret \(\widehat{\sigma}\) in context.
\[\text{RSS} = 2^2 + 0^2 + (-2)^2 + (-2)^2 + 0^2 + 2^2 = 16\]

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
Q3: Errors vs. Residuals; Unbiasedness
(b) What does it mean to say the OLS estimators are unbiased? Why is unbiasedness a desirable property?

An estimator is unbiased if its expected value equals the true parameter:
\[E(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \beta_1 \qquad E(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \beta_0\]
On average across many repeated samples, the estimates are correct.

text:
Summary

CI for mean response at \(x^*\): targets \(E(Y \mid X = x^*)\)
PI for new observation at \(x^*\): targets an individual \(Y^*\); adds \(\sigma^2\) for irreducible noise — always wider than the CI; does not shrink to zero as \(n \to \infty\)
Both intervals are centered at \(\widehat{Y}^*\) and are narrowest at \(x^* = \bar{X}\), widening with extrapolation
ANOVA: SST = SSR + SSE; F-test uses \(F^* = \text{MSR}/\text{MSE} \sim F(1, n-2)\); equivalent to the t-test via \(F^* = (t^*)^2\)
\(R^2\): fraction of variance explained; always increases with more predictors so we use \(\bar{R}^2\) for model comparison

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
Sampling Distribution of \(\widehat{\beta}_0\)
Since \(\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{Y} - \widehat{\beta}_1 \bar{X}\), it is also a linear combination of the \(Y_i\)’s, so it is normal.

We previously showed: \(E(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \beta_0\) and \(\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \sigma^2\!\left(\dfrac{1}{n} + \dfrac{\bar{X}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\)
\[\boxed{\widehat{\beta}_0 \sim N\!\left(\beta_0,\ \sigma^2\!\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar{X}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\right)}\]

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
From Normal to \(t\)

Standardization: subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation: \[Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma}\]
Standardizing \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) gives a standard normal:
\[\frac{\widehat{\beta}_1 - \beta_1}{\sigma / S_{xx}^{1/2}} \sim N(0, 1)\]
The problem: \(\sigma^2\) is unknown. We replace it with \(\text{MSE} = \dfrac{\text{RSS}}{n-2}\).

Replacing a fixed constant with a random estimate inflates the tails. The result is no longer normal.
Recall from last lecture: \(T = Z / (V/k)^{1/2}\) where \(Z \sim N(0,1)\) and \(V \sim \chi^2_k\). The missing piece is showing that RSS fits the chi-squared structure in the denominator:
\[\frac{\text{RSS}}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-2} \quad \text{and is independent of } \widehat{\beta}_0 \text{ and } \widehat{\beta}_1\]

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
section: From Normal to \(t\): Putting It Together (Solution)
text:
From Normal to \(t\): Putting It Together (Solution)

We have two pieces:

\(\dfrac{\widehat{\beta}_1 - \beta_1}{\sigma / S_{xx}^{1/2}} \sim N(0,1)\) — the standardized slope
\(\dfrac{\text{RSS}}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-2}\), independent of \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) — the chi-squared denominator

Step 1: The statistic we want — replace unknown \(\sigma\) with \(\sqrt{\text{MSE}}\):
\[\frac{\widehat{\beta}_1 - \beta_1}{(\text{MSE}/S_{xx})^{1/2}}\]
Step 2: Divide numerator and denominator by \(\sigma/S_{xx}^{1/2}\):
\[\frac{\widehat{\beta}_1 - \beta_1}{(\text{MSE}/S_{xx})^{1/2}} = \frac{\dfrac{\widehat{\beta}_1 - \beta_1}{\sigma/S_{xx}^{1/2}}}{\dfrac{(\text{MSE}/S_{xx})^{1/2}}{\sigma/S_{xx}^{1/2}}} = \frac{\dfrac{\widehat{\beta}_1 - \beta_1}{\sigma/S_{xx}^{1/2}}}{\left(\dfrac{\text{MSE}}{\sigma^2}\right)^{1/2}}\]
Step 3: Substitute \(\text{MSE} = \text{RSS}/(n-2)\) to expose the \(\chi^2\) piece:
\[= \frac{\dfrac{\widehat{\beta}_1 - \beta_1}{\sigma/S_{xx}^{1/2}}}{\left(\dfrac{\text{RSS}/\sigma^2}{n-2}\right)^{1/2}}\]
Step 4: Label each piece — numerator \(\sim N(0,1)\); denominator \(\sim \left(\chi^2_{n-2}/(n-2)\right)^{1/2}\), independent of numerator:
\[\text{Numerator: } \frac{\widehat{\beta}_1 - \beta_1}{\sigma/S_{xx}^{1/2}} \sim N(0,1) \qquad \text{Denominator: } \sqrt{\frac{\text{RSS}/\sigma^2}{n-2}} \sim \sqrt{\frac{\chi^2_{n-2}}{n-2}}\]
Step 5: By the definition of the \(t\) distribution, \(T = Z / \sqrt{V/k}\) where \(Z \sim N(0,1)\), \(V \sim \chi^2_k\), independent:
\[\frac{\widehat{\beta}_1 - \beta_1}{(\text{MSE}/S_{xx})^{1/2}} \sim t_{n-2}\]

section: Confidence Interval and Hypothesis Test for \(\beta_0\)
text:
Confidence Interval and Hypothesis Test for \(\beta_0\)

Let \(\text{SE}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \left[\text{MSE}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{n} + \dfrac{\bar{X}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\right]^{1/2}\)
Confidence interval: A \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI for \(\beta_0\):
\[\widehat{\beta}_0 \;\pm\; t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-2} \cdot \text{SE}(\widehat{\beta}_0)\]

Hypothesis test: To test \(H_0: \beta_0 = \beta_{00}\) vs. \(H_1: \beta_0 \neq \beta_{00}\) (or one-sided), compute:
\[t^* = \frac{\widehat{\beta}_0 - \beta_{00}}{\text{SE}(\widehat{\beta}_0)} \sim t_{n-2} \text{ under } H_0\]

Decision rules at significance level \(\alpha\):







Hypotheses
Reject \(H_0\) if




\(H_1: \beta_1 \neq \beta_{10}\) (two-sided)
\(|t^*| > t_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-2}\)


\(H_1: \beta_1 > \beta_{10}\) (right-sided)
\(t^* > t_{1-\alpha,\, n-2}\)


\(H_1: \beta_1 < \beta_{10}\) (left-sided)
\(t^* < -t_{1-\alpha,\, n-2}\)

2. Fitting the Model and Extracting Key Quantities
Fit the model and inspect the summary() output. The summary() gives a preview of inference results. We will reconstruct each piece manually in the sections that follow.

fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
summary(fit)

Extract key quantities that are used throughout the rest of the lab. Confirm this chunk runs without errors before continuing.

n      <- nrow(mtcars)
b0     <- coef(fit)["(Intercept)"]
b1     <- coef(fit)["wt"]
x      <- mtcars$wt
x_bar  <- mean(x)
RSS    <- sum(residuals(fit)^2)

MSE    <- RSS / (n - 2)

title: Lab 3: Inference in Simple Linear Regression
text:
3. MLE vs. OLS Estimate of \(\sigma^2\) (Lec 05)
From Lecture 5, the two estimates of the error variance are:
\[\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\text{OLS}} = \frac{\text{RSS}}{n - 2} = \text{MSE} \qquad \text{(unbiased)}\]
\[\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{\text{RSS}}{n} \qquad \text{(biased — does not correct for the two estimated parameters)}\]
Compute both estimates and display them side by side. Notice which estimate is larger and whether this matches the direction of bias described above.

sigma2_OLS <- RSS / (n - 2)
sigma2_MLE <- RSS / n

data.frame(
  Estimator = c("OLS (unbiased)", "MLE (biased)"),
  Formula   = c("RSS / (n - 2)", "RSS / n"),
  Value     = round(c(sigma2_OLS, sigma2_MLE), 3)
) |>
  kable(align = "llr", caption = "Comparing OLS and MLE estimates of σ²")

title: Lab 3: Inference in Simple Linear Regression
text:
4. The \(t\)-Distribution and Critical Values (Lec 05/06)
From Lecture 5, if \(Z \sim N(0,1)\) and \(V \sim \chi^2_k\) independently, then
\[T = \frac{Z}{\sqrt{V / k}} \sim t_k\]
In regression, replacing the unknown \(\sigma^2\) with MSE produces exactly this structure:
\[\frac{\widehat{\beta}_1 - \beta_1}{(\text{MSE}/S_{xx})^{1/2}} \sim t_{n-2}\]

4.1 Visualizing the \(t\)-Distribution
The chunk below overlays several distributions. Pay attention to how the tails compare across different degrees of freedom.

x_vals <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 500)

df_dist <- data.frame(
  x    = rep(x_vals, 4),
  y    = c(dnorm(x_vals),
           dt(x_vals, df = 5),
           dt(x_vals, df = 10),
           dt(x_vals, df = n - 2)),
  dist = rep(c("Normal", "t (df = 5)", "t (df = 10)",
               paste0("t (df = ", n - 2, ", our model)")),
             each = 500)
)

ggplot(df_dist, aes(x = x, y = y, color = dist)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(title = "t-Distribution vs. Normal",
       x = NULL, y = "Density", color = "Distribution") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Lecture 7: Inference in Regression
text: Normality Assumption and MLE

title: Lecture 7: Inference in Regression
text:
Why Normality?
So far we have focused on point estimation — no distributional assumption was needed.
For inference (confidence intervals and hypothesis tests), we need the sampling distribution of \(b_0\) and \(b_1\).

We now adopt the normality model:
\[Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon_i, \quad \varepsilon_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathrm{N}(0, \sigma^2), \quad i = 1, \ldots, n\]
This implies \(Y_i \sim \mathrm{N}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i,\; \sigma^2)\).


This is stronger than the Gauss-Markov assumptions, which only required:

\(\mathrm{E}(\varepsilon_i) = 0\), \(\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma^2\) (homoscedasticity)
Uncorrelated errors



Under normality the distribution is fully specified — so we can write down a likelihood function.

title: Lecture 7: Inference in Regression
text:
Maximum Likelihood Estimation
Since \(Y_i \sim \mathrm{N}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i,\; \sigma^2)\), the joint likelihood for \(n\) independent observations is:
\[L(\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma^2) = \frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{n/2}} \exp\!\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i)^2\right\}\]

The log-likelihood is easier to maximize:
\[\ell(\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma^2) = -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi) - \frac{n}{2}\log\sigma^2 - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i)^2\]


The MLEs \(\hat\beta_0\), \(\hat\beta_1\) maximize \(\ell\) by minimizing the last term — which is exactly the least-squares criterion.

Key result: Under normality, MLE = OLS for \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\).

title: Lecture 7: Inference in Regression
text:
MLE of \(\sigma^2\)
Setting \(\partial\ell/\partial\sigma^2 = 0\) gives:
\[\hat{\sigma}^2_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)^2 = \frac{\text{SSE}}{n}\]




Estimator
Formula
Unbiased?




\(\hat\sigma^2_{\text{MLE}}\)
\(\text{SSE}/n\)
No


MSE
\(\text{SSE}/(n-2)\)
Yes



The MLE divides by \(n\) instead of \(n - 2\), losing two degrees of freedom for estimating \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\).


We always use MSE for inference. The MLE of \(\sigma^2\) is biased and is mentioned here because it appears in theoretical derivations.

title: Lecture 7: Inference in Regression
text: Inference on \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\)

title: Lecture 7: Inference in Regression
text:
Sampling Distribution of \(b_1\)
We can write \(b_1 = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i Y_i\) where \(c_i = (X_i - \bar{X})/S_{xx}\) — a linear combination of the normal \(Y_i\)’s.

Since linear combinations of independent normals are normal, with \(\mathrm{E}(b_1) = \beta_1\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(b_1) = \sigma^2/S_{xx}\):
\[b_1 \sim \mathrm{N}\!\left(\beta_1,\; \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}\right), \qquad S_{xx} = \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2\]


Two additional results (without proof):

\(\text{SSE}/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-2}\)
\(\text{SSE}\) is independent of \(b_0\) and \(b_1\)



Replacing \(\sigma^2\) with MSE \(= \text{SSE}/(n-2)\) gives the t-pivot:
\[\frac{b_1 - \beta_1}{\sqrt{\text{MSE}/S_{xx}}} \sim t_{n-2}\]

title: Lecture 7: Inference in Regression
text:
Confidence Interval for \(\beta_1\)
From the \(t_{n-2}\) pivot, a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI for \(\beta_1\) is:
\[\boxed{b_1 \;\pm\; t_{1-\alpha/2,\; n-2}\sqrt{\frac{\text{MSE}}{S_{xx}}}}\]

The term \(\sqrt{\text{MSE}/S_{xx}}\) is the standard error of \(b_1\) — reported in R as Std. Error next to the slope.



fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
confint(fit, level = 0.95)

                2.5 %    97.5 %
(Intercept) 33.450500 41.119753
wt          -6.486308 -4.202635




The 95% CI for \(\beta_1\) does not contain 0 — significant evidence of a negative relationship between weight and fuel efficiency.

title: Lecture 7: Inference in Regression
text:
Hypothesis Test for \(\beta_1\)
To test \(H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_{10}\) vs. \(H_1: \beta_1 \neq \beta_{10}\):
\[t^* = \frac{b_1 - \beta_{10}}{\sqrt{\text{MSE}/S_{xx}}} \sim t_{n-2} \text{ under } H_0\]
Reject \(H_0\) if \(|t^*| > t_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-2}\).

The most common test is \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) (no linear relationship):
\[t^* = \frac{b_1}{\sqrt{\text{MSE}/S_{xx}}}\]
This is the t value column in summary(lm(...)).



summary(fit)$coefficients

             Estimate Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 37.285126   1.877627 19.857575 8.241799e-19
wt          -5.344472   0.559101 -9.559044 1.293959e-10

title: Lecture 7: Inference in Regression
text:
Inference for \(\beta_0\)
By similar arguments:
\[b_0 \sim \mathrm{N}\!\left(\beta_0,\; \sigma^2\!\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar{X}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\right)\]

The \(t\)-pivot:
\[\frac{b_0 - \beta_0}{\sqrt{\text{MSE}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{n} + \dfrac{\bar{X}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)}} \sim t_{n-2}\]


A \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI for \(\beta_0\):
\[\boxed{b_0 \;\pm\; t_{1-\alpha/2,\; n-2}\sqrt{\text{MSE}\!\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar{X}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)}}\]
Hypothesis tests for \(\beta_0\) follow the same structure as for \(\beta_1\).

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text: Analysis of Variance

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Partitioning Total Variation
Every observation’s deviation from \(\bar{Y}\) splits into two parts:
\[Y_i - \bar{Y} = (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i) + (\hat{Y}_i - \bar{Y})\]

Squaring and summing over all \(i\):
\[\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \bar{Y})^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[(Y_i - \hat{Y}_i) + (\hat{Y}_i - \bar{Y})\right]^2\]
\[= \sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)^2 + \sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{Y}_i - \bar{Y})^2 + 2\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)(\hat{Y}_i - \bar{Y})\]


The cross-product term is zero. Writing \(e_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\):
\[\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)(\hat{Y}_i - \bar{Y})\]
\[= \sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)\hat{Y}_i - \sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)\bar{Y}\]
\[= \sum_{i=1}^n e_i \hat{Y}_i - \bar{Y}\sum_{i=1}^n e_i = 0\]
because \(\sum_{i=1}^n e_i = 0\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^n e_i \hat{Y}_i = 0\) both follow from the normal equations.

\(\mathrm{E}(\text{MSR}) = \sigma^2 + \beta_1^2 S_{xx}\) — MSR has two pieces: \(\sigma^2\) (noise, always present) plus \(\beta_1^2 S_{xx}\) (signal from the slope, only present when \(\beta_1 \neq 0\))

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
The F-Test

Goal: Test \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) vs. \(H_1: \beta_1 \neq 0\) to test if there is any linear relationship between \(X\) and \(Y\).

Intuition: If \(\beta_1 \neq 0\), the model should explain a lot of variation, so SSR should be large relative to SSE. But SSR alone depends on the scale of \(Y\) — a “large” SSR in one dataset might be tiny in another. We need a relative measure.


The F-statistic: Compare each SS scaled by its degrees of freedom (a mean square):
\[F^* = \frac{\text{MSR}}{\text{MSE}} = \frac{\text{SSR}/1}{\text{SSE}/(n-2)}\]


Why does this work? Recall from the ANOVA table:










\(\mathrm{E}(\text{MSR})\)
\(\mathrm{E}(\text{MSE})\)

Under \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\)
\(\sigma^2\)
\(\sigma^2\)

Under \(H_1: \beta_1 \neq 0\)
\(\sigma^2 + \beta_1^2 S_{xx}\)
\(\sigma^2\)
\(\gg 1\)



A large \(F^*\) means the model explains far more than noise alone would.

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
\(R^2\) and Adjusted \(R^2\)

The coefficient of determination measures the fraction of variation in \(Y\) explained by the model:
\[R^2 = \frac{\text{SSR}}{\text{SST}} = 1 - \frac{\text{SSE}}{\text{SST}} \;\in\; [0, 1]\]
The equality follows directly from SST = SSR + SSE — dividing both sides by SST gives \(1 = \frac{\text{SSR}}{\text{SST}} + \frac{\text{SSE}}{\text{SST}}\), so \(\frac{\text{SSR}}{\text{SST}} = 1 - \frac{\text{SSE}}{\text{SST}}\).

Adding any predictor always increases \(R^2\) — it can be inflated by irrelevant variables.


Adjusted \(R^2\) penalizes for the number of \(\beta\) parameters \(p\) (\(p = 2\) in SLR):
\[\bar{R}^2 = 1 - \frac{\text{SSE}/(n-p)}{\text{SST}/(n-1)}\]
\(\bar{R}^2\) can decrease when a weak predictor is added, making it preferred for model comparison.

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Where We Left Off
In Lectures 5 and 6, we:

Added the normality assumption \(\varepsilon_i \overset{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2)\) and derived MLE (Lecture 5)
Used the \(t_{n-2}\) pivot to build CIs and hypothesis tests for \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) (Lecture 6)


Today we extend inference in two new directions:

Prediction — quantify uncertainty when making predictions at a new \(x^*\). Two distinct questions: what do we expect on average, vs. what will one specific new observation be?
Model fit — partition total variation into what the model explains (SSR) vs. what remains (SSE); use this to test \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) via an F-test and summarize fit with \(R^2\).

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
section: The Setup: New Points and Randomness
text:
The Setup: New Points and Randomness

What is \(x^*\)? A new, fixed input value — not one of the \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) used to fit the model. The \(*\) marks it as “new.”

Example: A study fits lm(Mort ~ Lat) on 49 US states, where Mort is skin cancer mortality (deaths per 10 million) and Lat is latitude in degrees north. A new state enters at 40° north latitude: \(x^* = 40\). What can we say about its cancer mortality?

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Estimation of Mean Response
We want to estimate \(E(Y^*) = E(Y \mid X = x^*)\) — the mean response at a new input \(x^*\).
An obvious estimate is:
\[\widehat{Y}^* = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x^*\]

Since \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) are both linear combinations of the normal \(Y_i\)’s, \(\widehat{Y}^*\) also follows a normal distribution.
To build a confidence interval, we follow the same strategy as Lecture 6: find the mean and variance of \(\widehat{Y}^*\), standardize to get a \(t\)-pivot, then invert.

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Sampling Distribution of \(\widehat{Y}_h\)

We need to first confirm \(\widehat{Y}_h\) is unbiased, and then derive \(\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{Y}_h)\).
\(\mathrm{E}(\widehat{Y}_h) = \mathrm{E}(\widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x^*) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x^*\) ✓

For the variance, substitute \(\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{Y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{X}\):
\[\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{Y}_h) = \mathrm{Var}(\bar{Y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{X} + \widehat{\beta}_1 x^*) = \mathrm{Var}(\bar{Y} + \widehat{\beta}_1(x^* - \bar{X}))\]


Expanding:
\[= \mathrm{Var}(\bar{Y}) + (x^* - \bar{X})^2\,\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) + 2(x^* - \bar{X})\,\mathrm{Cov}(\bar{Y},\, \widehat{\beta}_1)\]


Substituting known variances from Lectures 5–6:
\[\mathrm{Var}(\bar{Y}) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}\]


The cross-term vanishes because \(\mathrm{Cov}(\bar{Y}, \widehat{\beta}_1) = 0\) (shown on the next slide):
\[= \frac{\sigma^2}{n} + (x^* - \bar{X})^2 \cdot \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} = \sigma^2\!\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x^* - \bar{X})^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\]

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Why \(\mathrm{Cov}(\bar{Y},\, b_1) = 0\)?
Recall \(b_1 = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i Y_i\) where \(a_i = (X_i - \bar{X})/S_{xx}\).
\[\mathrm{Cov}(\bar{Y},\, b_1) = \mathrm{Cov}\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i,\; \sum_{i=1}^n a_i Y_i\right)\]

Since the \(Y_i\) are independent, only the \(i = j\) terms survive:
\[= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,\mathrm{Var}(Y_i) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\]


And \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n a_i = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{X_i - \bar{X}}{S_{xx}} = \frac{1}{S_{xx}}\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})}_{=\;0} = 0\)
Therefore \(\mathrm{Cov}(\bar{Y}, b_1) = 0\). \(\square\)

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Sampling Distribution of \(\widehat{Y}_h\) — Result

We now have both pieces — the mean and the variance. Putting them together gives the full sampling distribution, which we then standardize into a \(t\)-pivot to construct the CI:
\[\widehat{Y}_h \sim N\!\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x^*,\;\; \sigma^2\!\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x^* - \bar{X})^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\right)\]

Replacing \(\sigma^2\) with MSE gives the \(t_{n-2}\) pivot:
\[\frac{\widehat{Y}_h - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x^*)}{\sqrt{\text{MSE}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{n} + \dfrac{(x^*-\bar{X})^2}{S_{xx}}\right)}} \sim t_{n-2}\]


A \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for \(E(Y \mid X = x^*)\):
\[\boxed{\widehat{Y}_h \;\pm\; t_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-2}\sqrt{\text{MSE}\!\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x^*-\bar{X})^2}{S_{xx}}\right)}}\]

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Why \(\mathrm{Cov}(\bar{Y},\, \widehat{\beta}_1) = 0\)?
Recall \(\widehat{\beta}_1 = \sum_{j=1}^n a_j Y_j\) where \(a_j = (X_j - \bar{X})/S_{xx}\).
\[\mathrm{Cov}(\bar{Y},\, \widehat{\beta}_1) = \mathrm{Cov}\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i,\; \sum_{j=1}^n a_j Y_j\right) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n a_j\,\mathrm{Cov}(Y_i, Y_j)\]

Since the \(Y_i\) are independent, \(\mathrm{Cov}(Y_i, Y_j) = 0\) for \(i \neq j\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(Y_i) = \sigma^2\) for \(i = j\), so only the diagonal terms survive:
\[= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,\mathrm{Var}(Y_i) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\]


And \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n a_i = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{X_i - \bar{X}}{S_{xx}} = \frac{1}{S_{xx}}\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})}_{=\;0} = 0\)
Therefore \(\mathrm{Cov}(\bar{Y}, \widehat{\beta}_1) = 0\). \(\square\)

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
section: Worked Example: Skin Cancer and Latitude
text:
Worked Example: Skin Cancer and Latitude

Background: Researchers collected skin cancer mortality rates (deaths per 10 million) and latitude (degrees north) for \(n = 49\) US states. Higher latitudes receive less direct sunlight, so we expect mortality to decrease as latitude increases. A simple linear regression was fit, yielding:
\[\widehat{\text{Mort}} = 389.19 - 5.978 \times \text{Lat}, \qquad \bar{X} = 39.5°\]
Question: A new state is being added to the dataset with latitude \(x^* = 41°\) north. We want to quantify uncertainty about its cancer mortality — both for the average state at that latitude and for this specific new state.

Point estimate at \(x^* = 41°\):
\[\widehat{Y}^* = 389.19 - 5.978(41) = \mathbf{144.1} \text{ deaths per 10 million}\]
predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(Lat = 41), interval = "confidence")
#      fit      lwr      upr
#  144.092  138.361  149.823
95% CI: We are 95% confident the average mortality for all states at 41° north is between 138.4 and 149.8 deaths per 10 million.


predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(Lat = 41), interval = "prediction")
#      fit      lwr      upr
#  144.092  105.212  182.972
95% PI: We predict this specific new state at 41° north will have mortality between 105.2 and 183.0 deaths per 10 million. Notice how this range is nearly 7× wider than the CI — the extra width captures the individual-level noise \(\varepsilon^*\) that no amount of data can reduce.

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Width Depends on Distance from \(\bar{X}\)

The CI formula contains \(\dfrac{(x^* - \bar{X})^2}{S_{xx}}\) — this grows as \(x^*\) moves away from \(\bar{X}\).

For the skin cancer model with \(\bar{X} = 39.5°\):

The interval at 28° is nearly 3× wider, even though \(n\) is the same.


Takeaway: Intervals are narrowest at \(\bar{X}\) and widen with extrapolation. The further you predict from the center of your data, the less certain you should be.

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Two Prediction Questions

After fitting \(\widehat{Y} = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 X\), we often want to say something about a new input value \(x^*\).
The point estimate \(\widehat{Y}^* = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x^*\) is the same regardless — but to build an interval, we first need to ask: what exactly are we trying to capture? The answer leads to two fundamentally different questions:

Question 1 — Mean response: > “What is the average cancer mortality for all US states at 40° latitude?”
Targets \(E(Y \mid X = x^*) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x^*\) — a fixed (unknown) parameter.
\(\longrightarrow\) Confidence interval for mean response


Question 2 — New individual observation: > “What will skin cancer mortality be in this specific state at 40° latitude?”
Targets \(Y^* = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x^* + \varepsilon^*\) — a random variable with its own noise.
\(\longrightarrow\) Prediction interval

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
From Prediction to Model Assessment
So far we have focused on making predictions at a specific \(x^*\) and building intervals around them.

A separate question is: how well does the model fit the data overall?

Does the predictor \(X\) explain a meaningful share of the variation in \(Y\)?
Is there statistical evidence of any linear relationship?



Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) answers this by decomposing the total variation in \(Y\) into two parts:

What the model explains — variation in the fitted values \(\hat{Y}_i\) around \(\bar{Y}\)
What the model does not explain — the residuals \(Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\)

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Whats Random and whats not?


Why is \(Y\) random? The model \(Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon_i\) treats the \(X_i\) as fixed; \(Y_i\) is random because \(\varepsilon_i \sim N(0,\sigma^2)\).


At \(x^*\), keep these three things straight:








Quantity
Random?
Why




\(\widehat{Y}^* = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x^*\)
Yes
\(x^*\) is fixed, but \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) were estimated from random training data — a different sample gives different \(\widehat{\beta}_0, \widehat{\beta}_1\), and thus a different \(\widehat{Y}^*\)


\(\varepsilon^*\)
Yes
New individual noise — independent of the training data


\(E(Y \mid X = x^*) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x^*\)
No
The true \(\beta_0, \beta_1\) are fixed constants (we just don’t know them)



This is why we need two different types of intervals — one for the fixed mean, one for a new individual observation. We define them on the next slide.

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Sampling Distribution of \(\widehat{Y}^*\)

We need to first confirm \(\widehat{Y}^*\) is unbiased, and then derive \(\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{Y}^*)\).
\(\mathrm{E}(\widehat{Y}^*) = \mathrm{E}(\widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x^*) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x^*\) ✓

For the variance, substitute \(\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{Y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{X}\):
\[\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{Y}^*) = \mathrm{Var}(\bar{Y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{X} + \widehat{\beta}_1 x^*) = \mathrm{Var}(\bar{Y} + \widehat{\beta}_1(x^* - \bar{X}))\]


Expanding using \(\mathrm{Var}(A + cB) = \mathrm{Var}(A) + c^2\,\mathrm{Var}(B) + 2c\,\mathrm{Cov}(A, B)\) with \(A = \bar{Y}\), \(B = \widehat{\beta}_1\), \(c = x^* - \bar{X}\):
\[= \mathrm{Var}(\bar{Y}) + (x^* - \bar{X})^2\,\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) + 2(x^* - \bar{X})\,\mathrm{Cov}(\bar{Y},\, \widehat{\beta}_1)\]


Substituting known variances from Lectures 5–6:
\[\mathrm{Var}(\bar{Y}) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}\]


The cross-term vanishes because \(\mathrm{Cov}(\bar{Y}, \widehat{\beta}_1) = 0\) (shown on the next slide):
\[= \frac{\sigma^2}{n} + (x^* - \bar{X})^2 \cdot \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} = \sigma^2\!\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x^* - \bar{X})^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\]

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Sampling Distribution of \(\widehat{Y}^*\) — Result

We now have both pieces — the mean and the variance. Putting them together gives the full sampling distribution, which we then standardize into a \(t\)-pivot to construct the CI:
\[\widehat{Y}^* \sim N\!\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x^*,\;\; \sigma^2\!\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x^* - \bar{X})^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\right)\]

Replacing \(\sigma^2\) with MSE gives the \(t_{n-2}\) pivot:
\[\frac{\widehat{Y}^* - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x^*)}{\sqrt{\text{MSE}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{n} + \dfrac{(x^*-\bar{X})^2}{S_{xx}}\right)}} \sim t_{n-2}\]


A \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for \(E(Y \mid X = x^*)\):
\[\boxed{\widehat{Y}^* \;\pm\; t_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-2}\sqrt{\text{MSE}\!\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x^*-\bar{X})^2}{S_{xx}}\right)}}\]

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Partitioning Total Variation — Result
Dropping the cross-product term gives:
\[\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \bar{Y})^2}_{\text{SST}} = \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{Y}_i - \bar{Y})^2}_{\text{SSR}} + \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)^2}_{\text{SSE}}\]




Symbol
Name
Meaning




SST
Total SS
Total variation in \(Y\)


SSR
Regression SS
Variation explained by \(X\)


SSE
Error SS
Variation unexplained (residual) — same as RSS

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
The F-Test — Decision Rule

Under \(H_0\), \(F^* \sim F(1,\, n-2)\). Reject \(H_0\) at level \(\alpha\) if:
\[F^* > F(1-\alpha;\; 1,\, n-2)\]
where \(F(1-\alpha;\; 1,\, n-2)\) is the \((1-\alpha)\) quantile of the \(F(1, n-2)\) distribution.


fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
anova(fit)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: mpg
          Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
wt         1 847.73  847.73  91.375 1.294e-10 ***
Residuals 30 278.32    9.28                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1





n <- nrow(mtcars)
qf(0.95, df1 = 1, df2 = n - 2)

[1] 4.170877


Since \(F^* = 91.4 > 4.17 = F(0.95;\; 1,\, 30)\), we reject \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\). There is strong evidence of a linear relationship between vehicle weight and fuel efficiency.

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Why \(\mathrm{E}(\text{MSR}) = \sigma^2 + \beta_1^2 S_{xx}\)?
Start from \(SSR = \sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{Y}_i - \bar{Y})^2\). Since \(\bar{Y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1\bar{X}\):
\[\hat{Y}_i - \bar{Y} = (\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_i) - (\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1\bar{X}) = \hat{\beta}_1(X_i - \bar{X})\]

Therefore:
\[SSR = \sum_{i=1}^n \hat{\beta}_1^2(X_i - \bar{X})^2 = \hat{\beta}_1^2\, S_{xx}\]
Since \(\text{MSR} = \text{SSR}/1\): \(\quad E(\text{MSR}) = S_{xx}\, E(\hat{\beta}_1^2)\)


Use the identity \(E(\hat{\beta}_1^2) = \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1) + [E(\hat{\beta}_1)]^2 = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} + \beta_1^2\):
\[E(\text{MSR}) = S_{xx}\!\left(\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} + \beta_1^2\right) = \sigma^2 + \beta_1^2 S_{xx}\]


When \(\beta_1 = 0\): \(E(\text{MSR}) = \sigma^2 = E(\text{MSE})\) — both estimate the same thing.
When \(\beta_1 \neq 0\): \(E(\text{MSR}) > \sigma^2\) — MSR is inflated, so \(F^* = \text{MSR}/\text{MSE}\) will tend to be large.

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
The F Distribution

The F distribution is the distribution of a ratio of two independent chi-squared random variables, each divided by their degrees of freedom:
\[F(d_1, d_2) = \frac{\chi^2_{d_1}/d_1}{\chi^2_{d_2}/d_2}\]

In our setting:

\(\text{SSR}/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_1\) — we showed \(\text{SSR} = \hat{\beta}_1^2 S_{xx}\); under \(H_0\), \(\hat{\beta}_1\sqrt{S_{xx}}/\sigma \sim N(0,1)\), and squaring a standard normal gives \(\chi^2_1\)
\(\text{SSE}/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-2}\) — same result as \(\text{RSS}/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-2}\) stated in Lec 6 (SSE = RSS)
These two are independent



Taking their ratio:
\[F^* = \frac{\text{SSR}/\sigma^2 \;/\; 1}{\text{SSE}/\sigma^2 \;/\; (n-2)} = \frac{\text{SSR}/1}{\text{SSE}/(n-2)} \sim F(1,\, n-2) \quad \text{under } H_0\]
The \(\sigma^2\)’s cancel — we do not need to know \(\sigma^2\) to use the test.


The F distribution is always non-negative and right-skewed. We only reject \(H_0\) for large values of \(F^*\), because a large ratio means the model explains far more variation than noise alone would.

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Roadmap: Three Types of Intervals

In Lecture 6 we built intervals about the parameters of the line. Today we build intervals about predicted values.









What it targets
Question it answers




CI for \(\beta_1\) (Lec 6)
The true slope \(\beta_1\)
“How steep is the relationship between x and y, and is there evidence it’s non-zero?”


CI for \(\beta_0\) (Lec 6)
The true intercept \(\beta_0\)
“Where does the line cross \(X = 0\)?”


CI for mean response (today)
\(E(Y \mid X = x^*) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x^*\)
“What is the average \(Y\) for all units at \(x^*\)?”


Prediction interval (today)
A new individual \(Y^* = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x^* + \varepsilon^*\)
“What will this specific new observation be at \(x^*\)?”




Key shift: Lecture 6 asked what the line looks like. Today we ask what the line predicts at a new point and whether we want the average outcome or one individual outcome.

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Deriving \(\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{Y}^*)\) (Solution, Steps 1–3)

Step 1: Confirm unbiasedness:
\[\mathrm{E}(\widehat{Y}^*) = \mathrm{E}(\widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x^*) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x^* \checkmark\]
Step 2: Substitute \(\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{Y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{X}\):
\[\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{Y}^*) = \mathrm{Var}(\bar{Y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{X} + \widehat{\beta}_1 x^*) = \mathrm{Var}(\bar{Y} + \widehat{\beta}_1(x^* - \bar{X}))\]
Step 3: Apply \(\mathrm{Var}(A + cB) = \mathrm{Var}(A) + c^2\,\mathrm{Var}(B) + 2c\,\mathrm{Cov}(A,B)\) with \(A = \bar{Y}\), \(B = \widehat{\beta}_1\), \(c = x^* - \bar{X}\):
\[= \mathrm{Var}(\bar{Y}) + (x^* - \bar{X})^2\,\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) + 2(x^* - \bar{X})\,\mathrm{Cov}(\bar{Y},\, \widehat{\beta}_1)\]

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Deriving \(\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{Y}^*)\) (Solution, Steps 4–5)

Step 4: Substitute known variances from Lectures 5–6:
\[\mathrm{Var}(\bar{Y}) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}\]
\[= \frac{\sigma^2}{n} + (x^* - \bar{X})^2 \cdot \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} + 2(x^* - \bar{X})\,\mathrm{Cov}(\bar{Y},\, \widehat{\beta}_1)\]
Step 5: The cross-term vanishes because \(\mathrm{Cov}(\bar{Y}, \widehat{\beta}_1) = 0\) (shown on the next slide):
\[\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{Y}^*) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n} + (x^* - \bar{X})^2 \cdot \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} = \sigma^2\!\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x^* - \bar{X})^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\]

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Partitioning Total Variation (Steps 1–3)

Step 1: Write the deviation decomposition for a single observation — split \(Y_i - \bar{Y}\) into two pieces:



Step 2: Square both sides and sum over all \(i\). Expand the square — you should get three terms:



Step 3: Let \(e_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\). Show the cross-product term equals zero by splitting it and applying the two normal equation results: \(\sum e_i = 0\) and \(\sum e_i \hat{Y}_i = 0\):

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Partitioning Total Variation (Solution)

Step 1: Every observation’s deviation from \(\bar{Y}\) splits into two parts:
\[Y_i - \bar{Y} = (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i) + (\hat{Y}_i - \bar{Y})\]
Step 2: Square and sum over all \(i\):
\[\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \bar{Y})^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)^2 + \sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{Y}_i - \bar{Y})^2 + 2\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)(\hat{Y}_i - \bar{Y})\]
Step 3: The cross-product term is zero. Writing \(e_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\):
\[\sum_{i=1}^n e_i(\hat{Y}_i - \bar{Y}) = \sum_{i=1}^n e_i \hat{Y}_i - \bar{Y}\sum_{i=1}^n e_i = 0 - 0 = 0\]
because \(\sum e_i \hat{Y}_i = 0\) and \(\sum e_i = 0\) both follow from the normal equations. Dropping the cross-product gives SST = SSR + SSE.


Why is \(\sum e_i \hat{Y}_i = 0\)? Substitute \(\hat{Y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_i\) and factor out the constants:
\[\sum_{i=1}^n e_i \hat{Y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 \sum_{i=1}^n e_i + \hat{\beta}_1 \sum_{i=1}^n e_i X_i = \hat{\beta}_0 \cdot 0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \cdot 0 = 0\]
Both sums are zero by properties 1 and 3 of OLS residuals from Lecture 4: \(\sum e_i = 0\) (from \(\partial\text{RSS}/\partial\hat{\beta}_0 = 0\)) and \(\sum e_i X_i = 0\) (from \(\partial\text{RSS}/\partial\hat{\beta}_1 = 0\)). So \(\sum e_i \hat{Y}_i = 0\) is not a separate fact — it is a linear combination of those two normal equation conditions.

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Why \(\mathrm{E}(\text{MSR}) = \sigma^2 + \beta_1^2 S_{xx}\)? (Steps 1–3)

Step 1: Start from \(\text{SSR} = \sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{Y}_i - \bar{Y})^2\). Use \(\bar{Y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1\bar{X}\) to simplify \(\hat{Y}_i - \bar{Y}\):



Step 2: Substitute back into SSR and factor to write \(\text{SSR} = \hat{\beta}_1^2 S_{xx}\). Then use \(\text{MSR} = \text{SSR}/1\) to write \(\mathrm{E}(\text{MSR})\) in terms of \(\mathrm{E}(\hat{\beta}_1^2)\):



Step 3: Apply the identity \(\mathrm{E}(\hat{\beta}_1^2) = \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1) + [\mathrm{E}(\hat{\beta}_1)]^2\) and substitute the known variance and mean of \(\hat{\beta}_1\) to reach the final result:

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Why \(\mathrm{E}(\text{MSR}) = \sigma^2 + \beta_1^2 S_{xx}\)? (Solution)

Step 1: Since \(\bar{Y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1\bar{X}\):
\[\hat{Y}_i - \bar{Y} = (\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_i) - (\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1\bar{X}) = \hat{\beta}_1(X_i - \bar{X})\]
Step 2: Substitute back and factor:
\[\text{SSR} = \sum_{i=1}^n \hat{\beta}_1^2(X_i - \bar{X})^2 = \hat{\beta}_1^2\, S_{xx}\]
Since \(\text{MSR} = \text{SSR}/1\): \(\quad \mathrm{E}(\text{MSR}) = S_{xx}\,\mathrm{E}(\hat{\beta}_1^2)\)
Step 3: Apply \(\mathrm{E}(\hat{\beta}_1^2) = \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1) + [\mathrm{E}(\hat{\beta}_1)]^2 = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} + \beta_1^2\):
\[\mathrm{E}(\text{MSR}) = S_{xx}\!\left(\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} + \beta_1^2\right) = \sigma^2 + \beta_1^2 S_{xx}\]

section: Confidence Interval and Prediction Interval in R
text:
Confidence Interval and Prediction Interval in R

fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)

# 95% CI: average mpg for all cars weighing 3500 lbs
predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(wt = 3.5),
        interval = "confidence", level = 0.95)

       fit      lwr      upr
1 18.57948 17.43342 19.72553




# 95% PI: mpg for one new specific car weighing 3500 lbs
predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(wt = 3.5),
        interval = "prediction", level = 0.95)

       fit      lwr      upr
1 18.57948 12.25426 24.90469




The fit (fit) is identical. The PI is wider because the only change is adding individual-level noise.

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Worked Example: Skin Cancer & Lat

Background: Researchers collected skin cancer mortality rates (deaths per 10 million) and latitude (degrees north) for \(n = 49\) US states. Higher latitudes receive less direct sunlight, so we expect mortality to decrease as latitude increases. A simple linear regression was fit, yielding:
\[\widehat{\text{Mort}} = 389.19 - 5.978 \times \text{Lat}, \qquad \bar{X} = 39.5°\]
Question: A new state is being added to the dataset with latitude \(x^* = 41°\) north. We want to quantify uncertainty about its cancer mortality — both for the average state at that latitude and for this specific new state.

Point estimate at \(x^* = 41°\):
\[\widehat{Y}^* = 389.19 - 5.978(41) = \mathbf{144.1} \text{ deaths per 10 million}\]
predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(Lat = 41), interval = "confidence")
#      fit      lwr      upr
#  144.092  138.361  149.823
95% CI: We are 95% confident the average mortality for all states at 41° north is between 138.4 and 149.8 deaths per 10 million.


predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(Lat = 41), interval = "prediction")
#      fit      lwr      upr
#  144.092  105.212  182.972
95% PI: We predict this specific new state at 41° north will have mortality between 105.2 and 183.0 deaths per 10 million. Notice how this range is nearly 7× wider than the CI — the extra width captures the individual-level noise \(\varepsilon^*\) that no amount of data can reduce.

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Connection to the t-Test
In simple linear regression, the F-test for \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) and the two-sided t-test for \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) are exactly equivalent — they always produce the same p-value. This follows from the identity:
\[F^* = (t^*)^2\]
Squaring a \(t_{n-2}\) random variable gives an \(F(1, n-2)\) random variable, so the critical values are also linked: \(F(1-\alpha;\; 1,\, n-2) = \left[t_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-2}\right]^2\).

Practical implication: In simple linear regression you can use either test — they are the same test. The F-test becomes essential in multiple regression, where it tests whether any predictor is useful rather than just one slope.

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of today you will be able to:


Explain why model diagnostics are necessary before performing inference
Identify the four key assumptions of simple linear regression and which residual plot checks each
Read and interpret residual-vs-fitted and QQ-plots to detect assumption violations
Describe remedial measures for nonlinearity, nonconstant variance, and non-independence

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Where We Left Off
In Lectures 5–7, we:

Derived the sampling distributions of \(\widehat{\beta}_0\), \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) under the normality assumption
Built confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for the parameters
Partitioned variation into SSR + SSE and introduced the F-test for \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\)
Constructed CIs for mean response and prediction intervals for new observations


All of that inference is only valid if the model assumptions hold.
Today we ask: how do we check them? And if they fail, what do we do?

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text: Diagnostics

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
The Need for Diagnostics
After fitting a regression model it is important to determine whether all the necessary model assumptions are valid before performing inference.

If there are any violations, subsequent inferential procedures may lead to faulty conclusions.
Therefore, it is crucial to perform appropriate model diagnostics.


We also want to check for:

Outliers — points far from the fitted model
Influential observations — points that disproportionately affect the fit
Omitted predictors — important variables left out of the model

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
The Four Assumptions
The linear regression model \(Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon_i\) assumes \(\varepsilon_i \overset{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2)\).
This single statement encodes four assumptions (in order of importance):









#
Assumption
What it means




1
Linearity
\(E(Y) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X\)


2
Independence
Responses \(Y_i\) are independent of each other


3
Equal variance
\(\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma^2\) for all \(i\)


4
Normality
Errors \(\varepsilon_i\) follow a normal distribution





Usually we are not certain in advance whether these hold. We need to check them before performing inference or prediction.

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Residuals as Diagnostic Tools
Recall the residuals \(e_i = Y_i - \widehat{Y}_i\).

\(e_i\) can be regarded as the observed error of \(\varepsilon_i\).
Since several assumptions concern \(\varepsilon_i\) — e.g., \(E(\varepsilon_i) = 0\), independence, equal variance, normality — we use the residuals \(e_i\) to check these assumptions.

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Four Residual Plots








Plot
Checks
What to look for




Residuals vs. \(X\)
Assumption 1 (linearity)
A systematic curve or trend indicates nonlinearity


Residuals vs. time order
Assumption 2 (independence)
A trend over time indicates correlated errors — only relevant when data have a time order


Residuals vs. fitted \(\widehat{Y}\)
Assumption 3 (equal variance)
A fan shape (variance growing with \(\widehat{Y}\)) indicates heteroscedasticity


QQ-plot
Assumption 4 (normality)
Systematic deviation from the diagonal indicates non-normality

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Prototype Residual Plots

Top-left is the ideal pattern — random scatter around zero with no trend and constant spread.

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
The QQ-Plot (Normal Probability Plot)
If \(\varepsilon_1, \ldots, \varepsilon_n \overset{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2)\), consider the order statistics \(e_{(1)} \leq e_{(2)} \leq \cdots \leq e_{(n)}\). Then:
\[E(e_{(k)}) \approx \sqrt{\text{MSE}}\; z\!\left(\frac{k - 0.375}{n + 0.25}\right)\]
where \(z(A)\) denotes the \(A \times 100\) percentile of the standard normal distribution.

The QQ-plot shows residuals (vertical axis) versus approximated expected normal quantiles (horizontal axis).
We expect the points to fall reasonably close to a straight line when the errors are close to normal.

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
QQ-Plots When Not Normal



U-shaped (skewed right): Points curve above the line in both tails — right-skewed distribution
U-shaped (skewed left): Points curve below the line — left-skewed distribution
S-shaped: Points deviate outward at both extremes — heavier tails than normal

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Outliers in Residual Plots

An outlier is a point that is far away from the model. It stands out clearly in residual plots and/or the QQ-plot.












How to handle outliers:

Correct or discard if it is a data-entry error
Sometimes the outlier itself is of singular interest (a rare event worth studying)
Do not automatically exclude outliers — try sensitivity analysis and/or robust methods

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Beer Data: Diagnostic Plots

Recall: BAC (blood alcohol content) was regressed on number of beers consumed (\(n = 16\)).


beer <- data.frame(
  beers = c(5,2,9,8,3,7,3,5,3,5,4,6,5,7,1,4),
  bac   = c(0.10,0.03,0.19,0.12,0.04,0.095,0.07,0.06,0.02,0.05,0.07,0.10,0.085,0.09,0.01,0.05)
)
fit_beer <- lm(bac ~ beers, data = beer)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
plot(beer$beers, residuals(fit_beer), xlab = "Number of beers", ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs predictor", pch = 16, col = "#003660"); abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
plot(fitted(fit_beer), residuals(fit_beer), xlab = "Fitted", ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs fitted", pch = 16, col = "#003660"); abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
qqnorm(residuals(fit_beer), main = "QQ-plot", pch = 16, col = "#003660"); qqline(residuals(fit_beer))




The residuals show no strong pattern — random scatter, roughly constant spread, and points close to the QQ line. The linearity and normality assumptions appear reasonably satisfied here.

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
section: F Test for Lack of Fit
text: F Test for Lack of Fit

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Testing Linearity Formally
The residual plots give us a visual check on Assumption 1. But can we test whether the linear relationship fits adequately?

Yes — when there are replicated observations (multiple \(Y\) values at the same \(X\) value), we can use an F test for lack of fit.
The idea: compare the fit of - a full model that allows any mean function (one-way ANOVA) - a restricted model that imposes the linear relationship \(E(Y) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X\)

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Extra Sum of Squares Principle

The general framework for comparing nested models:

Fit the full model \(\rightarrow\) error sum of squares \(SSE(F)\)
Fit the restricted model \(\rightarrow\) error sum of squares \(SSE(R)\)
\(SSE(R) \geq SSE(F)\) always — the full model always fits at least as well



The extra sum of squares \(SSE(R) - SSE(F)\) measures the additional error incurred by the restriction. It should be small when \(H_0\) is true.
The F statistic: \[F^* = \frac{[SSE(R) - SSE(F)] / (df_R - df_F)}{SSE(F)/df_F} \overset{H_0}{\sim} F_{df_R - df_F,\; df_F}\]
Reject \(H_0\) if \(F^* > F(1-\alpha;\; df_R - df_F,\; df_F)\)

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Setup: Replicated Observations

Denote \(X_1, \ldots, X_c\) as the \(c\) distinct observed values of \(X\).

\(j\) indexes each distinct \(X\) value (\(j = 1, \ldots, c\))
\(i\) indexes the replicates for a given \(X_j\) (\(i = 1, \ldots, n_j\))
\(n_j\) = number of \(Y\) values at \(X_j\)

The full dataset:
\[n_1 \text{ replicates at } X_1: Y_{11}, \ldots, Y_{n_1 1}\] \[n_2 \text{ replicates at } X_2: Y_{12}, \ldots, Y_{n_2 2}\] \[\vdots\] \[n_c \text{ replicates at } X_c: Y_{1c}, \ldots, Y_{n_c c}\]
Total observations: \(n = \sum_{j=1}^c n_j\)

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
section: Full Model and Pure Error SS
text:
Full Model and Pure Error SS
Full model (one-way ANOVA — no linearity assumption):
\[Y_{ij} = \mu_j + \varepsilon_{ij}, \quad j = 1, \ldots, c;\; i = 1, \ldots, n_j, \quad \varepsilon_{ij} \overset{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2)\]

The LS estimates of \(\mu_j\) are the group means \(\bar{Y}_j = \sum_{i=1}^{n_j} Y_{ij}/n_j\).
Pure error sum of squares (within-group variation):
\[SSPE = SSE(F) = \sum_{j=1}^c \sum_{i=1}^{n_j} (Y_{ij} - \bar{Y}_j)^2, \qquad df_F = n - c\]
This is pure error because it measures variation around group means — completely free of any linearity assumption.

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
section: Restricted Model and Lack of Fit SS
text:
Restricted Model and Lack of Fit SS
Restricted model (linear regression — imposes linearity):
\[Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_j + \varepsilon_{ij}, \qquad df_R = n - 2\]

Let \(\widehat{Y}_{ij} = b_0 + b_1 X_j\) be the fitted values. Then \(SSE(R) = \sum_{j}\sum_i (Y_{ij} - \widehat{Y}_{ij})^2\).
Key decomposition:
\[SSE(R) = SSPE + SSLF\]
where the lack of fit sum of squares is:
\[SSLF = \sum_{j=1}^c \sum_{i=1}^{n_j} (\bar{Y}_j - \widehat{Y}_{ij})^2 = \sum_{j=1}^c n_j(\bar{Y}_j - \widehat{Y}_{ij})^2, \qquad df_{LF} = c - 2\]


SSLF measures how far the group means deviate from the fitted line — it is zero only if the line passes perfectly through every group mean.

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
section: The F Test for Lack of Fit
text:
The F Test for Lack of Fit
Applying the extra sum of squares principle:
\[F^* = \frac{[SSE(R) - SSE(F)]/(df_R - df_F)}{SSE(F)/df_F} = \frac{SSLF/(c-2)}{SSPE/(n-c)} = \frac{MSLF}{MSPE} \overset{H_0}{\sim} F_{c-2,\; n-c}\]

Decision rule: Reject \(H_0\) (i.e., reject the linear model) if \(F^* > F(1-\alpha;\; c-2,\; n-c)\).
This F test is also called the pure error test.

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Practice: Lack of Fit Test

An experiment has \(c = 4\) distinct \(X\) values with \(n_2 = 3\) replicates each (\(n = 12\)). After fitting the linear regression and the full ANOVA model:

\(SSE(R) = 480.2\) (linear model)
\(SSE(F) = SSPE = 120.4\) (pure error)

(a) Compute \(SSLF\) and its degrees of freedom.
(b) Compute \(MSLF\) and \(MSPE\).
(c) Compute \(F^*\) and state whether you reject the linear model at \(\alpha = 0.05\). Critical value: \(F(0.95;\; 2,\; 8) = 4.46\).
(d) What does this result tell you about Assumption 1?

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
section: Practice: Lack of Fit Test — Solution
text:
Practice: Lack of Fit Test — Solution
(a) \(SSLF = SSE(R) - SSE(F) = 480.2 - 120.4 = 359.8\)
\(df_{LF} = c - 2 = 4 - 2 = 2\); \(\quad df_{PE} = n - c = 12 - 4 = 8\)

(b) \[MSLF = \frac{359.8}{2} = 179.9 \qquad MSPE = \frac{120.4}{8} = 15.05\]


(c) \[F^* = \frac{MSLF}{MSPE} = \frac{179.9}{15.05} = 11.95\]
Since \(11.95 > 4.46\), we reject the linear model at \(\alpha = 0.05\).


(d) There is statistically significant evidence that the linear function does not adequately fit the data — Assumption 1 (linearity) appears to be violated. We should consider a transformation or a more flexible model.

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text: Remedial Measures

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
section: What to Do When Assumptions Fail
text:
What to Do When Assumptions Fail
When the linear regression model is not appropriate, there are two general approaches:

1. Develop a more appropriate model

Polynomial regression: \(E(Y) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \beta_2 X^2\)
Nonlinear regression: \(E(Y) = \beta_0 \beta_1^X\)
Nonparametric regression: \(E(Y) = f(X)\) where \(f\) is estimated from data
These can be more flexible but also more complex



2. Transformation

Transform \(X\), \(Y\), or both to make the linear model more appropriate
Usually relatively simple — keeps the familiar OLS framework
Common transformations: \(\sqrt{\cdot}\), \(\log(\cdot)\), \(\exp(\cdot)\), \(1/(\cdot)\)

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Remedies by Assumption







Violated assumption
Remedy




Linearity
Transform \(X\) or \(Y\); add polynomial terms; use nonlinear/nonparametric model


Independence
Correlated-error models (time series, mixed models) — not covered in this course


Equal variance
Weighted least squares; variance-stabilizing transformation of \(Y\)


Normality
Variance-stabilizing transformation of \(Y\) often helps both at once




On outliers:

Investigate the cause before deciding what to do
If a data-entry error: correct or remove
If a real data point: do not remove automatically; run the analysis with and without the outlier (sensitivity analysis) or use robust regression

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text: Transformations

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
When and How to Transform
We can transform \(X\) and/or \(Y\) and hope that the linear regression model is adequate for the transformed variables.

Transformations of \(X\) — address nonlinearity while leaving error variance roughly unchanged:







Shape of relationship
Try




Concave up (fast growth)
\(X' = X^2\) or \(X' = e^X\)


Concave down (diminishing returns)
\(X' = \log(X)\) or \(X' = \sqrt{X}\)


Decreasing, convex
\(X' = 1/X\) or \(X' = e^{-X}\)





Transformations of \(Y\) — address nonconstant variance and/or nonnormality:
\[Y' = \sqrt{Y}, \qquad Y' = \log_{10}(Y), \qquad Y' = 1/Y\]
These are called variance-stabilizing transformations.

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Box-Cox: Choosing the Transformation of \(Y\)
It is often difficult to determine which transformation is most appropriate from diagnostic plots alone. The Box-Cox method selects a power transformation data-adaptively.

Suppose \(Y > 0\). Consider the family:
\[Y(\lambda) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{Y^\lambda - 1}{\lambda} & \lambda \neq 0 \\ \log Y & \lambda = 0 \end{cases}\]
where \(\lambda\) is treated as a parameter to be estimated.


We hope that \(Y(\lambda)\) satisfies:

\(E(Y(\lambda)) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X\)
\(\mathrm{Var}(Y(\lambda)) = \sigma^2\) (constant)
\(Y(\lambda)\) is approximately normal

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Box-Cox: Estimating \(\lambda\)
Treating \(Y(\lambda) \overset{\text{approx}}{\sim} N(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X, \sigma^2)\), the profiled log-likelihood (after maximizing over \(\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma^2\) for fixed \(\lambda\)) is:
\[\ell_p(\lambda) = -\frac{n}{2}\log\!\left\{\frac{SSE(\lambda)}{n}\right\} + (\lambda - 1)\sum_{i=1}^n \log Y_i\]
where \(SSE(\lambda)\) is the residual sum of squares after fitting \(Y(\lambda) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X\).

The MLE of \(\lambda\) is the value that maximizes \(\ell_p(\lambda)\).
In practice:

Plot \(\ell_p(\lambda)\) vs \(\lambda\) and find the peak
An approximate \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence region for \(\lambda\): \(\{\lambda : \ell_p(\hat\lambda) - \ell_p(\lambda) \leq \frac{1}{2}\chi^2_1(1-\alpha)\}\)
Round \(\hat\lambda\) to a nearby interpretable value (e.g., \(0.5 \to \sqrt{Y}\), \(0 \to \log Y\), \(-1 \to 1/Y\))

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Box-Cox in R

library(MASS)
fit_faithful2 <- lm(eruptions ~ waiting, data = faithful)
boxcox(fit_faithful2, lambda = seq(-1, 2, len = 100))




The peak is near \(\hat\lambda \approx 1\), and the 95% confidence region comfortably includes \(\lambda = 1\) (no transformation). This suggests the original scale is adequate for the Old Faithful data — consistent with the mostly clean residual plots we saw earlier.

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Practice: Full Workflow

A researcher regresses pollution level \(Y\) (ppb) on distance from factory \(X\) (km) using \(n = 40\) observations.

The residual-vs-fitted plot shows a clear decreasing fan (large residuals at small fitted values, small residuals at large fitted values)
The QQ-plot shows a strong right-skew (points curve above the line)
The lack of fit F test gives \(F^* = 1.2\), \(p = 0.35\)

(a) Which assumptions appear violated? Which appears satisfied?
(b) What transformation of \(Y\) would you try first, and why?
(c) After a \(\log(Y)\) transformation, the residual-vs-fitted plot looks ideal. Write the fitted model (in terms of \(\log Y\)) and explain how you would predict \(Y\) for a new \(X = 5\) km.

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Practice: Full Workflow — Solution
(a)

Equal variance (Assumption 3): Violated — the fan shape in the residual-vs-fitted plot indicates nonconstant variance.
Normality (Assumption 4): Violated — right-skew in the QQ-plot.
Linearity (Assumption 1): Satisfied — the lack of fit test does not reject the linear model (\(p = 0.35\)).


(b) Try \(Y' = \log(Y)\). A log transformation is the natural choice for right-skewed data with a fan-pattern (variance growing with the mean), which often arises when \(Y > 0\) and spans several orders of magnitude.


(c) The fitted model after transformation: \(\widehat{\log Y} = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 X\).
To predict \(Y\) at \(X = 5\): compute \(\widehat{\log Y}^* = \widehat{\beta}_0 + 5\widehat{\beta}_1\), then back-transform: \(\widehat{Y}^* = e^{\widehat{\log Y}^*}\).

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Summary

Diagnostics: Check all four assumptions (linearity, independence, equal variance, normality) using residual-vs-X, residual-vs-fitted, residual-vs-time, and QQ-plots before performing inference
Outliers: Investigate first — don’t automatically remove
Remedial measures: Two broad options — develop a more appropriate model, or apply a transformation

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Plot 1: Residuals vs. \(X\)
Checks: Assumption 1 — Linearity
What to look for: Random scatter around zero with no trend is ideal. A systematic curve or pattern remaining in the residuals after fitting indicates the linear function does not adequately capture the relationship.

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Plot 2: Residuals vs. Time Order

Checks: Assumption 2 — Independence
The x-axis is the sequential order observations were collected (row 1, row 2, …, row \(n\)) — or actual timestamps if available.
What to look for: Random scatter with no trend is ideal. A systematic drift or cyclical pattern suggests correlated errors — each observation’s error is related to previous ones. Only construct this plot when data have a natural collection order.

Correlated errors do not bias \(\hat{\beta}\) but invalidate standard errors, \(t\)-tests, and \(F\)-tests.

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Plot 3: Residuals vs. Fitted \(\widehat{Y}\)
Checks: Assumption 3 — Equal variance
What to look for: Constant spread around zero across all fitted values is ideal. A fan shape (spread increasing or decreasing with \(\widehat{Y}\)) indicates heteroscedasticity (nonconstant variance).

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Plot 4: QQ-Plot (Normal Probability Plot)
Checks: Assumption 4 — Normality
The QQ-plot compares the observed residuals (y-axis) to the quantiles you would expect if the errors were perfectly normal (x-axis). R computes the expected quantiles automatically.

What to look for: Points falling close to the diagonal reference line indicate normally distributed errors. Systematic departures signal non-normality:

U-shaped curve: skewed distribution (right- or left-skewed)
S-shaped curve: heavier tails than normal

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Old Faithful: Diagnostic Plots
Data: faithful (built into R) — \(n = 272\) eruptions of the Old Faithful geyser. We regress eruption duration (\(Y\), minutes) on waiting time between eruptions (\(X\), minutes).

fit_faithful <- lm(eruptions ~ waiting, data = faithful)

par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

# Plot 1: residuals vs X (checks linearity)
plot(faithful$waiting, residuals(fit_faithful),
     xlab = "Waiting time (min)", ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs X", pch = 16, col = "#003660"); abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

# Plot 3: residuals vs fitted (checks equal variance)
plot(fitted(fit_faithful), residuals(fit_faithful),
     xlab = "Fitted", ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs fitted", pch = 16, col = "#003660"); abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

# Plot 4: QQ-plot (checks normality)
qqnorm(residuals(fit_faithful), main = "QQ-plot", pch = 16, col = "#003660")
qqline(residuals(fit_faithful))

text:
Old Faithful: Diagnostic Plots — Output


Both residual plots show a slight bimodal clustering — the data has two natural groups (short and long eruptions), and a single line doesn’t capture this perfectly. The QQ-plot tails deviate modestly from the line, consistent with this mild non-normality.

Remedy




Linearity
Transform \(X\) or \(Y\); add polynomial terms; use nonlinear/nonparametric model


Independence
Correlated-error models (time series, mixed models) — not covered in this course


Equal variance
Weighted least squares; variance-stabilizing transformation of \(Y\)


Normality
Variance-stabilizing transformation of \(Y\) often helps both at once




On outliers:

Investigate the cause before deciding what to do
If a data-entry error: correct or remove
If a real data point: do not remove automatically; run the analysis with and without the outlier (sensitivity analysis) or use robust regression

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of today you will be able to:


Select an appropriate transformation of \(X\) or \(Y\) based on residual plot patterns
Use the Box-Cox method to data-adaptively choose a power transformation of \(Y\)
Back-transform predictions to the original scale after fitting a model on transformed \(Y\)
Apply the F test for lack of fit using the SSPE/SSLF decomposition to formally test whether a linear model is adequate
Explain the extra sum of squares principle and how it underlies the lack of fit F test

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
section: F Test for Lack of Fit
text: F Test for Lack of Fit

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
text:
Testing Linearity Formally
The residual plots give us a visual check on Assumption 1. But we can more formally test whether the linear relationship fits adequately.

When there are replicated observations (multiple \(Y\) values at the same \(X\) value), we can use an F test for lack of fit.
The idea: compare the fit of

a full model that allows any mean function (one-way ANOVA)
a restricted model that imposes the linear relationship \(E(Y) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X\)

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
text:
Extra Sum of Squares Principle

The general framework for comparing nested models:

Fit the full model \(\rightarrow\) obtain error sum of squares \(SSE(Full Model)\)
Fit the restricted model \(\rightarrow\) obtain error sum of squares \(SSE(Restricted Model)\)
\(SSE(R) \geq SSE(F)\) always — the full model always fits at least as well



The extra sum of squares \(SSE(R) - SSE(F)\) measures the additional error incurred by the restriction. It should be small when \(H_0\) is true.
The F statistic: \[F^* = \frac{[SSE(R) - SSE(F)] / (df_R - df_F)}{SSE(F)/df_F} \overset{H_0}{\sim} F_{df_R - df_F,\; df_F}\]
Reject \(H_0\) if \(F^* > F(1-\alpha;\; df_R - df_F,\; df_F)\)

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
text:
Setup: Replicated Observations

Denote \(X_1, \ldots, X_c\) as the \(c\) distinct observed values of \(X\).

\(j\) indexes each distinct \(X\) value (\(j = 1, \ldots, c\))
\(i\) indexes the replicates for a given \(X_j\) (\(i = 1, \ldots, n_j\))
\(n_j\) = number of \(Y\) values at \(X_j\)

The full dataset:
\[n_1 \text{ replicates at } X_1: Y_{11}, \ldots, Y_{n_1 1}\] \[n_2 \text{ replicates at } X_2: Y_{12}, \ldots, Y_{n_2 2}\] \[\vdots\] \[n_c \text{ replicates at } X_c: Y_{1c}, \ldots, Y_{n_c c}\]
Total observations: \(n = \sum_{j=1}^c n_j\)

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
section: Full Model and Pure Error SS
text:
Full Model and Pure Error SS
Full model (one-way ANOVA — no linearity assumption):
\[Y_{ij} = \mu_j + \varepsilon_{ij}, \quad j = 1, \ldots, c;\; i = 1, \ldots, n_j, \quad \varepsilon_{ij} \overset{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2)\]

The LS estimates of \(\mu_j\) are the group means \(\bar{Y}_j = \sum_{i=1}^{n_j} Y_{ij}/n_j\).
Pure error sum of squares (within-group variation):
\[SSPE = SSE(F) = \sum_{j=1}^c \sum_{i=1}^{n_j} (Y_{ij} - \bar{Y}_j)^2, \qquad df_F = n - c\]
This is pure error because it measures variation around group means — completely free of any linearity assumption.

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
section: Restricted Model and Lack of Fit SS
text:
Restricted Model and Lack of Fit SS
Restricted model (linear regression — imposes linearity):
\[Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_j + \varepsilon_{ij}, \qquad df_R = n - 2\]

Let \(\widehat{Y}_{ij} = b_0 + b_1 X_j\) be the fitted values. Then \(SSE(R) = \sum_{j}\sum_i (Y_{ij} - \widehat{Y}_{ij})^2\).
Key decomposition:
\[SSE(R) = SSPE + SSLF\]
where the lack of fit sum of squares is:
\[SSLF = \sum_{j=1}^c \sum_{i=1}^{n_j} (\bar{Y}_j - \widehat{Y}_{ij})^2 = \sum_{j=1}^c n_j(\bar{Y}_j - \widehat{Y}_{ij})^2, \qquad df_{LF} = c - 2\]


SSLF measures how far the group means deviate from the fitted line — it is zero only if the line passes perfectly through every group mean.

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
section: The F Test for Lack of Fit
text:
The F Test for Lack of Fit
Plugging the SSPE/SSLF decomposition into the extra SS framework gives the lack of fit F test (also called the pure error test):
\[F^* = \frac{SSLF/(c-2)}{SSPE/(n-c)} = \frac{MSLF}{MSPE} \overset{H_0}{\sim} F_{c-2,\; n-c}\]
Reject \(H_0\) (the linear model) when group means stray far from the fitted line relative to within-group noise.

\(SSE(R) = 14741.6\), \(\; df_R = n - 2 = 9\)

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
text:
Practice: Lack of Fit Test

An experiment has \(c = 4\) distinct \(X\) values with \(n_2 = 3\) replicates each (\(n = 12\)). After fitting the linear regression and the full ANOVA model:

\(SSE(R) = 480.2\) (linear model)
\(SSE(F) = SSPE = 120.4\) (pure error)

(a) Compute \(SSLF\) and its degrees of freedom.
(b) Compute \(MSLF\) and \(MSPE\).
(c) Compute \(F^*\) and state whether you reject the linear model at \(\alpha = 0.05\). Critical value: \(F(0.95;\; 2,\; 8) = 4.46\).
(d) What does this result tell you about Assumption 1?

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
section: Practice: Lack of Fit Test — Solution
text:
Practice: Lack of Fit Test — Solution
(a) \(SSLF = SSE(R) - SSE(F) = 480.2 - 120.4 = 359.8\)
\(df_{LF} = c - 2 = 4 - 2 = 2\); \(\quad df_{PE} = n - c = 12 - 4 = 8\)

(b) \[MSLF = \frac{359.8}{2} = 179.9 \qquad MSPE = \frac{120.4}{8} = 15.05\]


(c) \[F^* = \frac{MSLF}{MSPE} = \frac{179.9}{15.05} = 11.95\]
Since \(11.95 > 4.46\), we reject the linear model at \(\alpha = 0.05\).


(d) There is statistically significant evidence that the linear function does not adequately fit the data — Assumption 1 (linearity) appears to be violated. We should consider a transformation or a more flexible model.

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
text: Transformations

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
text:
When and How to Transform
We can transform \(X\) and/or \(Y\) and hope that the linear regression model is adequate for the transformed variables.

Transformations of \(X\) address nonlinearity while leaving error variance roughly unchanged:


Transformations of \(Y\) address nonconstant variance and/or nonnormality:
\[Y' = \sqrt{Y}, \qquad Y' = \log_{10}(Y), \qquad Y' = 1/Y\]
These are called variance-stabilizing transformations.

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
text:
Box-Cox: Choosing the Transformation of \(Y\)
When it’s hard to tell from a residual plot which transformation to use, Box-Cox finds it for you.

The idea: try every power transformation \(Y^\lambda\) for a range of \(\lambda\) values. For each \(\lambda\), fit the regression and measure how well the residuals behave. Pick the \(\lambda\) that gives the best fit.


Reading the output: boxcox() plots a likelihood curve over \(\lambda\). Find the peak, then round to the nearest interpretable value:



\(\hat\lambda\)
Transformation
Use when




1
none
residuals already look good


0.5
\(Y' = \sqrt{Y}\)
mild right skew / fan shape


0
\(Y' = \log Y\)
strong right skew / variance grows with mean


−1
\(Y' = 1/Y\)
severe right skew



The dashed lines on the plot show the 95% confidence interval for \(\lambda\) — if 1 is inside it, no transformation may be needed.



Under the hood: Box-Cox maximizes the profiled log-likelihood \(\ell_p(\lambda) = -\frac{n}{2}\log\{SSE(\lambda)/n\} + (\lambda-1)\sum \log Y_i\) over \(\lambda\), where \(SSE(\lambda)\) is the residual SS after fitting on \(Y^\lambda\).

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
text:
Box-Cox: Estimating \(\lambda\)
Treating \(Y(\lambda) \overset{\text{approx}}{\sim} N(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X, \sigma^2)\), the profiled log-likelihood (after maximizing over \(\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma^2\) for fixed \(\lambda\)) is:
\[\ell_p(\lambda) = -\frac{n}{2}\log\!\left\{\frac{SSE(\lambda)}{n}\right\} + (\lambda - 1)\sum_{i=1}^n \log Y_i\]
where \(SSE(\lambda)\) is the residual sum of squares after fitting \(Y(\lambda) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X\).

The MLE of \(\lambda\) is the value that maximizes \(\ell_p(\lambda)\).
In practice:

Plot \(\ell_p(\lambda)\) vs \(\lambda\) and find the peak
An approximate \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence region for \(\lambda\): \(\{\lambda : \ell_p(\hat\lambda) - \ell_p(\lambda) \leq \frac{1}{2}\chi^2_1(1-\alpha)\}\)
Round \(\hat\lambda\) to a nearby interpretable value (e.g., \(0.5 \to \sqrt{Y}\), \(0 \to \log Y\), \(-1 \to 1/Y\))

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
text:
Box-Cox in R
The trees dataset records girth, height, and timber volume for 31 black cherry trees. Volume is right-skewed — a natural candidate for transformation.

library(MASS)
fit_trees <- lm(Volume ~ Girth, data = trees)
boxcox(fit_trees, lambda = seq(-1, 2, len = 100))




The peak is near \(\hat\lambda \approx 0.3\) and the 95% CI excludes \(\lambda = 1\), so a transformation is warranted. Since 0 is inside the CI, we use \(Y' = \log(\text{Volume})\) — the nearest interpretable value.

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
text:
Practice: Full Workflow

A researcher regresses pollution level \(Y\) (ppb) on distance from factory \(X\) (km) using \(n = 40\) observations.

The residual-vs-fitted plot shows a clear decreasing fan (large residuals at small fitted values, small residuals at large fitted values)
The QQ-plot shows a strong right-skew (points curve above the line)
The lack of fit F test gives \(F^* = 1.2\), \(p = 0.35\)

(a) Which assumptions appear violated? Which appears satisfied?
(b) What transformation of \(Y\) would you try first, and why?
(c) After a \(\log(Y)\) transformation, the residual-vs-fitted plot looks ideal. Write the fitted model (in terms of \(\log Y\)) and explain how you would predict \(Y\) for a new \(X = 5\) km.

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
text:
Practice: Full Workflow — Solution
(a)

Equal variance (Assumption 3): Violated — the fan shape in the residual-vs-fitted plot indicates nonconstant variance.
Normality (Assumption 4): Violated — right-skew in the QQ-plot.
Linearity (Assumption 1): Satisfied — the lack of fit test does not reject the linear model (\(p = 0.35\)).


(b) Try \(Y' = \log(Y)\). A log transformation is the natural choice for right-skewed data with a fan-pattern (variance growing with the mean), which often arises when \(Y > 0\) and spans several orders of magnitude.


(c) The fitted model after transformation: \(\widehat{\log Y} = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 X\).
To predict \(Y\) at \(X = 5\): compute \(\widehat{\log Y}^* = \widehat{\beta}_0 + 5\widehat{\beta}_1\), then back-transform: \(\widehat{Y}^* = e^{\widehat{\log Y}^*}\).

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
text:
Summary

Transformations of \(X\): Fix nonlinearity (e.g., \(\log X\), \(\sqrt{X}\), \(X^2\)) while leaving error variance roughly unchanged
Transformations of \(Y\): Fix nonconstant variance and nonnormality simultaneously (e.g., \(\sqrt{Y}\), \(\log Y\)); these are variance-stabilizing transformations
Box-Cox: Estimates the optimal power \(\lambda\) for \(Y\) data-adaptively; round \(\hat\lambda\) to a nearby interpretable value (e.g., \(0.5 \to \sqrt{Y}\), \(0 \to \log Y\))
F test for lack of fit: When replicates exist, formally test \(H_0:\) linearity holds using \(F^* = MSLF/MSPE \sim F_{c-2,\; n-c}\); the key decomposition is \(SSE(R) = SSPE + SSLF\)
After transforming: Always re-check diagnostics on the transformed model; back-transform predictions to the original scale
Full workflow: Fit model \(\to\) check residual plots \(\to\) identify violations \(\to\) apply remedy \(\to\) re-check \(\to\) report

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Remedy 1: Nonlinearity
Violated assumption: Linearity — residuals vs. \(X\) show a curved pattern

Transform \(X\) — straightens a curved relationship while leaving error variance roughly unchanged:







Shape in scatter plot
Try




Concave up (fast growth)
\(X' = X^2\) or \(X' = e^X\)


Concave down (diminishing returns)
\(X' = \log(X)\) or \(X' = \sqrt{X}\)


Decreasing, convex
\(X' = 1/X\)





Add polynomial terms — e.g., \(E(Y) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \beta_2 X^2\) (covered later in the course)

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Remedy 2: Non-independence
Violated assumption: Independence — residuals vs. time order show a trend or cyclical pattern

Non-independence arises most often in time-series or spatial data, where nearby observations are correlated.
Correlated errors do not bias \(\hat{\beta}\) but invalidate standard errors, \(t\)-tests, and \(F\)-tests.


Remedies:

Correlated-error models — generalized least squares (GLS) with a structured covariance matrix
Time series models — ARIMA, autoregressive models
Mixed models — for clustered or repeated-measures data

These methods are not covered in this course, but it is important to recognize when they are needed.

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Remedy 3: Nonconstant Variance
Violated assumption: Equal variance — residuals vs. fitted \(\widehat{Y}\) show a fan shape

Variance-stabilizing transformation of \(Y\) — if variance grows with the mean, a transformation can stabilize it:



Pattern
Try




Mild
\(Y' = \sqrt{Y}\)


Moderate
\(Y' = \log(Y)\)


Strong
\(Y' = 1/\sqrt{Y}\)


Very strong
\(Y' = 1/Y\)



The Box-Cox method (Lecture 9) estimates the best power transformation data-adaptively.

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Remedy 4: Non-normality
Violated assumption: Normality — QQ-plot shows a U-shape (skewed) or S-shape (heavy tails)

Normality is the least critical assumption — OLS estimates are unbiased and consistent even without it. It mainly affects the validity of \(t\)- and \(F\)-tests in small samples.


Variance-stabilizing transformation of \(Y\) often fixes non-normality and nonconstant variance simultaneously (e.g., \(\log Y\), \(\sqrt{Y}\)).


When transformation is not enough:

Generalized linear models (GLMs) — model non-normal responses directly (e.g., Poisson for counts, logistic for binary outcomes)
Robust regression — less sensitive to heavy-tailed errors or outliers
For large \(n\), the CLT often makes the normality assumption less important in practice
