title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
section: Plot 1: What Produces a Curved Pattern?
text:
Plot 1: What Produces a Curved Pattern?

A curved residual pattern arises when the true relationship between \(X\) and \(Y\) is nonlinear but you fit a straight line.












The scatter plot (left) shows a concave-up (U-shaped) curve — the red line underfits in the middle and at the extremes. This mismatch produces the bowl-shaped residual pattern (right).

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Plot 2: What Produces Correlated Errors?
A drift pattern in residuals arises when observations collected over time influence each other — nearby values are more alike than distant ones.












The raw Y values (left) wander slowly over time rather than fluctuating randomly around the fit (red line). That drift survives into the residuals (right) as the correlated-errors violation.

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
section: Plot 3: What Produces a Fan Shape?
text:
Plot 3: What Produces a Fan Shape?
A fan shape in residuals arises when the spread of Y grows with X — larger X values have more variable responses.












The scatter plot (left) shows tightly clustered points at small X that fan outward as X increases. The red line fits well on average, but the growing spread carries into the residuals (right) as the fan-shape violation.

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
text:
Plot 4: What Produces Non-Normal Residuals?

A QQ-plot violation arises when the errors themselves have a skewed or heavy-tailed distribution rather than a bell curve.












The histogram (left) shows residuals bunched near zero with a long right tail — far from the symmetric bell curve (red). That asymmetry appears in the QQ-plot (right) as the U-shaped departure from the diagonal.

title: Lecture 8: Model Diagnostics and Remedial Measures
section: Old Faithful: What Do We Do?
text:
Old Faithful: What Do We Do?

Is this a serious violation? Not really — no strong curve, no fan shape, no dramatic QQ departure. The bimodal clustering is a feature of the data (two eruption types), not a model failure per se.

Verdict: the linear model is usable here, especially for prediction. The slope estimate and inference are not badly compromised. But we should be honest about what the model misses.


What could we do better?








Option
Idea
When to use it




Keep the linear model
Acknowledge the mild bimodality; use it for rough prediction
Sufficient for the research question


Add a group indicator
Create a short/long eruption category and include it as a predictor
When the two groups are substantively meaningful


Fit separate lines
One regression per group (short vs. long eruptions)
When the relationship differs between groups


Mixture model
Model the two-group structure explicitly
More advanced — beyond this course





Key takeaway: Diagnostic plots don’t always demand action — they demand judgment. Ask: how bad is it, and does it affect the conclusions I care about?

Practice: Reading Residual Plots — Solution
(a) Plot A — the spread of residuals increases with the fitted value (fan shape), violating equal variance (Assumption 3).

(b) Plot B — a curved trend remains in the residuals after fitting a line, violating linearity (Assumption 1).


(c) Plot C — random scatter around zero with no trend and roughly constant spread. This is the ideal pattern — no obvious violations.

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
section: F Test for Lack of Fit: Idea
text:
F Test for Lack of Fit: Idea

When there are replicated observations (multiple \(Y\) values at the same \(X\)), we can formally test whether the linear model is adequate using the extra sum of squares principle.
Compare two nested models:

Full model (one-way ANOVA, \(df_F = n-c\)): allows any mean function without linearity constraint
Restricted model (linear regression, \(df_R = n-2\)): imposes \(E(Y) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X\)


Since the full model is more flexible, \(SSE(R) \geq SSE(F)\) always. The extra sum of squares \(SSE(R) - SSE(F)\) quantifies the cost of imposing linearity — it should be small when the linear model is adequate.
\[F^* = \frac{[SSE(R) - SSE(F)] / (df_R - df_F)}{SSE(F)/df_F} \overset{H_0}{\sim} F_{df_R - df_F,\; df_F}\]
Reject \(H_0\) (reject the linear model) if \(F^* > F(1-\alpha;\; df_R - df_F,\; df_F)\).

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
text:
SSPE and SSLF Decomposition

Full model — one-way ANOVA: \(Y_{ij} = \mu_j + \varepsilon_{ij}\), estimated by group means \(\bar{Y}_j\).
\[SSPE \; (\textbf{Sum of Squares Pure Error}) = SSE(F) = \sum_{j=1}^c \sum_{i=1}^{n_j} (Y_{ij} - \bar{Y}_j)^2, \qquad df_F = n - c\]
Measures within-group variation without any linearity assumption.

Restricted model — linear regression: \(Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_j + \varepsilon_{ij}\), fitted values \(\widehat{Y}_{ij} = b_0 + b_1 X_j\), \(df_R = n-2\).
The key decomposition:
\[SSE(R) = SSPE + SSLF \; (\textbf{Sum of Squares Lack of Fit}) \qquad \text{where}
\qquad SSLF = \sum_{j=1}^c n_j(\bar{Y}_j - \widehat{Y}_{ij})^2, \quad df_{LF} = c - 2\]
SSLF measures how far group means stray from the fitted line. It is zero only if the line passes through every group mean.

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
text:
Full vs. Restricted Model

A group is all observations that share the same \(X\) value. Suppose we measure crop yield (\(Y\), bushels/acre) at three fertilizer doses (\(X\) = 10, 20, 30 g), with two plots at each dose. Each dose is a group.

Full model (one-way ANOVA) — predicts each group’s mean using only the observations in that group, with no connection across groups:
\[X = 10: Y = 15, 19 \;\Rightarrow\; \hat{Y} = 17 \qquad X = 20: Y = 22, 26 \;\Rightarrow\; \hat{Y} = 24 \qquad X = 30: Y = 28, 32 \;\Rightarrow\; \hat{Y} = 30\]
The model makes no claim about the relationship between these means.


Restricted model (linear regression) — forces all group means to fall on a single line \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X\). The predictions at \(X = 10\), \(20\), and \(30\) are now connected through the same slope and intercept — linearity is assumed.


Key insight: the difference \(SSE(R) - SSE(F) = SSLF\) is entirely due to the linearity constraint.

If the true relationship is linear: group means already fall near a line, so \(SSLF \approx 0\) and \(F^* \approx 1\)
If the true relationship is curved: group means stray from the fitted line, so \(SSLF\) is large and \(F^*\) is large

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
section: SSPE: Sum of Squares Pure Error
text:
SSPE: Sum of Squares Pure Error
\[SSPE = \sum_{j=1}^c \sum_{i=1}^{n_j} (Y_{ij} - \bar{Y}_j)^2, \qquad df_{PE} = n - c\]
Each term is the squared gap between one observation and its group mean.

This captures only natural within-group scatter. It is not referencing the fitted line at all. No matter what shape the true relationship is, SSPE stays the same. That is why it is called pure error.

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
section: SSLF: Sum of Squares Lack of Fit
text:
SSLF: Sum of Squares Lack of Fit
\[SSLF = \sum_{j=1}^c n_j(\bar{Y}_j - \widehat{Y}_j)^2, \qquad df_{LF} = c - 2\]
Each term is the squared gap between a group mean and the fitted line, weighted by group size.

This captures only the failure of linearity — how far the line misses each group mean. Within-group scatter plays no role. If the line passes through every group mean perfectly, \(SSLF = 0\).

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
section: SSE(R): Residuals from the Linear Model
text:
SSE(R): Residuals from the Linear Model
\[SSE(R) = \sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \widehat{Y}_i)^2, \qquad df_R = n - 2\]
Each term is the squared gap between one observation and the fitted line. This is the same RSS you already know from linear regression.

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
section: Linking the Three: SSE(R) = SSPE + SSLF
text:
Linking the Three: SSE(R) = SSPE + SSLF
Every observation’s deviation from the line can be split into two pieces:
\[\underbrace{(Y_i - \widehat{Y}_i)}_{\color{#D62728}{\text{obs to fitted line}}} = \underbrace{(Y_i - \bar{Y}_j)}_{\color{#1F77B4}{\text{obs to group mean}}} + \underbrace{(\bar{Y}_j - \widehat{Y}_i)}_{\color{#2CA02C}{\text{group mean to fitted line}}} \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad SSE(R) = SSPE + SSLF\]

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
text:
SSE(R), SSPE, and SSLF: Summary




Compares
Captures




\(SSE(R)\)
each obs vs. fitted line
total residual error


\(SSPE\)
each obs vs. group mean
pure within-group noise


\(SSLF\)
each group mean vs. fitted line
failure of linearity



The F test asks: is SSLF large relative to SSPE, or could it just be noise?

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
text:
Transformations of \(X\)
We can transform \(X\) and/or \(Y\) and hope that the linear regression model is adequate for the transformed variables.
Transformations of \(X\) address nonlinearity while leaving error variance roughly unchanged:







Shape of residual plot
Try




Concave up (fast growth)
\(X' = X^2\) or \(X' = e^X\)


Concave down (diminishing returns)
\(X' = \log(X)\) or \(X' = \sqrt{X}\)


Decreasing, convex
\(X' = 1/X\) or \(X' = e^{-X}\)

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
text:
Transformations of \(Y\)
Transformations of \(Y\) address nonconstant variance and/or nonnormality:
\[Y' = \sqrt{Y}, \qquad Y' = \log_{10}(Y), \qquad Y' = 1/Y\]
These are called variance-stabilizing transformations.

Unlike \(X\) transformations, transforming \(Y\) changes the error structure, so it can fix both non-constant variance and non-normality at once.
After fitting the model on \(Y'\), predictions must be back-transformed to the original scale (e.g., \(\widehat{Y} = (\widehat{Y}')^2\) after a square root transformation).

title: Lecture 9: Model Diagnostics — Formal Tests and Transformations
text:
Model Diagnostics: Overview
Before applying formal tests or transformations, recall the four assumptions of simple linear regression and how we check them:









Assumption
What it says
How to check




1. Linearity
\(E(Y \mid X) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X\)
Residual vs. fitted plot — no curve


2. Independence
Errors are uncorrelated
Study design / residual vs. order plot


3. Equal variance
\(\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma^2\) (constant)
Residual vs. fitted plot — no fan shape


4. Normality
\(\varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\)
Normal Q-Q plot — points on line





Today’s toolkit for when violations are found:

Nonlinearity → transform \(X\), or use the F test for lack of fit to confirm
Nonconstant variance / nonnormality → transform \(Y\) (Box-Cox can guide the choice)

title: Lab 4: Prediction, ANOVA, and Model Diagnostics
text:
Learning goals
In this lab, we will work with the Palmer Penguins dataset. Our main goals are:

Distinguish between confidence intervals for the mean response and prediction intervals for new observations.
Compute and visualize CI and PI bands using predict().
Partition variation using the ANOVA table and interpret \(R^2\).
Verify the \(F = t^2\) relationship in simple linear regression.
Check model assumptions using residual plots and QQ-plots.

title: Lab 4: Prediction, ANOVA, and Model Diagnostics
text:
Setup

library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
library(ggplot2)
library(skimr)

title: Lab 4: Prediction, ANOVA, and Model Diagnostics
text:
Load and inspect the data
We will again use the penguins dataset.

data("penguins")
head(penguins)

For this lab, we will focus on the variables:

body_mass_g: body mass in grams
bill_length_mm: bill length in millimeters
species: penguin species

Let us keep only the variables we need and remove missing values.

penguins_lab <- penguins %>%
  select(species, bill_length_mm, body_mass_g) %>%
  drop_na()

head(penguins_lab)


Quick visual review of the data

ggplot(penguins_lab, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Body Mass vs Bill Length",
    x = "Bill Length (mm)",
    y = "Body Mass (g)"
  )

Does the relationship look linear? Does the spread of points appear roughly constant across the range of bill lengths?

title: Lab 4: Prediction, ANOVA, and Model Diagnostics
text:
Fitting the model
We model body mass (body_mass_g) using bill length (bill_length_mm) as the predictor.

reg_fit <- lm(body_mass_g ~ bill_length_mm, data = penguins_lab)
summary(reg_fit)

title: Lab 4: Prediction, ANOVA, and Model Diagnostics
text:
Confidence and Prediction Intervals
When predicting at a new value \(x^*\), there are two distinct questions:

Confidence interval for the mean response: What is the average body mass for all penguins with bill length \(x^*\)? Uncertainty comes only from estimating the regression line.
Prediction interval for a new observation: What will the body mass of one new penguin with bill length \(x^*\) be? Uncertainty comes from both the estimated line and irreducible individual noise \(\varepsilon^*\).

The formulas are:
\[\text{CI: } \hat{Y}^* \pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-2}\sqrt{\text{MSE}\!\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x^* - \bar{X})^2}{S_{xx}}\right)}\]
\[\text{PI: } \hat{Y}^* \pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-2}\sqrt{\text{MSE}\!\left(1 + \frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x^* - \bar{X})^2}{S_{xx}}\right)}\]
The extra \(1\) under the radical in the PI accounts for the irreducible individual noise \(\varepsilon^*\).

Point prediction
Suppose a new penguin has bill length 45 mm.

new_penguin <- data.frame(bill_length_mm = 45)
predict(reg_fit, newdata = new_penguin)



Confidence interval for the mean response

predict(reg_fit, newdata = new_penguin, interval = "confidence", level = 0.95)


Question 1. Interpret this confidence interval in context.
Answer:



Prediction interval for a new observation

predict(reg_fit, newdata = new_penguin, interval = "prediction", level = 0.95)


Question 2. Compare the widths of the CI and PI. Which is wider? Why?
Answer:



Coding exercise
Obtain a 99% CI and 99% PI for a penguin with bill length 50 mm.

new_penguin2 <- data.frame(bill_length_mm = 50)

# TODO: compute 99% CI for the mean response at bill_length_mm = 50
ci_99 <- NULL

# TODO: compute 99% PI for a new observation at bill_length_mm = 50
pi_99 <- NULL



Visualizing both intervals

ci <- predict(reg_fit, interval = "confidence")
pi <- predict(reg_fit, interval = "prediction")

ggplot(penguins_lab, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = pi[, "lwr"], ymax = pi[, "upr"]), fill = "orange", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = ci[, "lwr"], ymax = ci[, "upr"]), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ci[, "fit"]), color = "firebrick", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Regression Line with Confidence and Prediction Bands",
    x = "Bill Length (mm)",
    y = "Body Mass (g)"
  )


Question 3. Where are the bands narrowest on the plot? What happens to the width of both intervals as \(x^*\) moves away from \(\bar{X}\)? What does this say about making predictions far from the center of the data?
Answer:

title: Lab 4: Prediction, ANOVA, and Model Diagnostics
text:
Analysis of Variance
ANOVA partitions the total variation in \(Y\) into a component explained by the model and a residual component:
\[\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \bar{Y})^2}_{\text{SST}} = \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{Y}_i - \bar{Y})^2}_{\text{SSR}} + \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)^2}_{\text{SSE}}\]

anova(reg_fit)

The ANOVA table includes:

Df: degrees of freedom (1 for model, \(n - 2\) for residuals)
Sum Sq: SSR and SSE
Mean Sq: \(\text{MSR} = \text{SSR}/1\), \(\text{MSE} = \text{SSE}/(n-2)\)
F value: \(F^* = \text{MSR}/\text{MSE}\)

Under \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\), \(F^* \sim F_{1,\, n-2}\). We reject \(H_0\) at level \(\alpha\) when \(F^*\) exceeds the critical value \(F_{1-\alpha;\, 1,\, n-2}\), found with qf().

n <- nrow(penguins_lab)
F_crit <- qf(0.95, df1 = 1, df2 = n - 2)
cat("Critical value:", round(F_crit, 4), "\n")


Question 4. Report the F-statistic from the ANOVA table. Compare it to the critical value above and state whether you reject \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\). State your conclusion in context.
Answer:


Extracting ANOVA components

anova_tbl <- anova(reg_fit)
SSR    <- anova_tbl[1, "Sum Sq"]
SSE    <- anova_tbl[2, "Sum Sq"]
SST    <- SSR + SSE
MSR    <- anova_tbl[1, "Mean Sq"]
MSE    <- anova_tbl[2, "Mean Sq"]
F_stat <- anova_tbl[1, "F value"]

cat("SSR =", round(SSR, 2), " SSE =", round(SSE, 2), " SST =", round(SST, 2), "\n")
cat("MSR =", round(MSR, 2), " MSE =", round(MSE, 2), " F =", round(F_stat, 2), "\n")



\(R^2\)
\(R^2 = \text{SSR}/\text{SST}\) is the proportion of total variation in \(Y\) explained by the model.

# TODO: compute R-squared as SSR / SST
R2 <- NULL
cat("R^2 =", round(R2, 4), "\n")

Verify against summary():

summary(reg_fit)$r.squared


Question 5. Interpret \(R^2\) in context. Does a high \(R^2\) guarantee the linear model is appropriate? Why or why not?
Answer:



Connection between \(F\) and \(t\)
In simple linear regression, \(F^* = (t^*)^2\). The F-test and the two-sided t-test for \(\beta_1 = 0\) always lead to the same conclusion.

t_from_model <- summary(reg_fit)$coefficients["bill_length_mm", "t value"]
cat("t^2 =", round(t_from_model^2, 2), "  F =", round(F_stat, 2), "\n")

title: Lab 4: Prediction, ANOVA, and Model Diagnostics
text:
Model Diagnostics
All inference (CIs, PIs, F-tests) is only valid if the model assumptions hold. The regression model \(Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon_i\) with \(\varepsilon_i \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2)\) encodes four assumptions:

Linearity: \(E(Y) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X\)
Independence: observations are uncorrelated
Equal variance (homoscedasticity): \(\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma^2\) for all \(i\)
Normality: \(\varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\)

We check these assumptions using residual plots. The key functions are residuals() for the residuals \(e_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\) and fitted() for the fitted values \(\hat{Y}_i\).

Plot 1: Residuals vs. \(X\) (linearity)
Random scatter around zero suggests linearity is met. A curved pattern indicates the true relationship is nonlinear.

plot(penguins_lab$bill_length_mm, residuals(reg_fit),
     xlab = "Bill Length (mm)", ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs X", pch = 16, col = "#003660")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)



Plot 2: Residuals vs. Fitted Values (equal variance)
Constant vertical spread suggests equal variance. A fan shape — spread increasing or decreasing with fitted values — indicates heteroscedasticity.

plot(fitted(reg_fit), residuals(reg_fit),
     xlab = "Fitted Values", ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs Fitted", pch = 16, col = "#003660")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)


Question 6. Examine both residual plots. Does the linearity assumption appear to be met? Does the equal variance assumption appear to be met? Describe any patterns you observe.
Answer:

Points near the diagonal indicate the residuals are approximately normally distributed. A U-shaped or S-shaped curve indicates departures from normality.
